title: Mailbox: CXL FPGA card does gather and filter near memory
idea: Like dropping a letter in a mailbox: the host writes a command descriptor to a mailbox region on an FPGA CXL memory card, the card gathers, filters or sparse-indexes rows locally, and only result lines return across the link. Built on an off-the-shelf FPGA CXL board.
why: Data movement: 5-20x fewer bytes over the link for embedding and graph lookups.

title: Memory-centric motherboard: compute cartridges plug into memory
idea: Reverse socket roles: the board is a mesh of DRAM modules and CXL/optical switches, and CPUs and accelerators are pluggable cartridges that attach to the memory regions they need. Memory stays installed for 8-10 years while compute is refreshed every 2.
why: Raises usable supply by ending DRAM disposal at each server refresh and recovering ~25-40% stranded DRAM, effectively 1.5-2x more usable bits from the same production.

title: Power by light, data by wire: photovoltaic-fed memory dies
idea: Swap delivery roles: a laser delivers power through a window or fibre onto photovoltaic cells on the top die of a memory stack, so the power TSVs that today outnumber signal TSVs can be repurposed for data.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): frees ~40-60% of TSVs; only viable for low-power capacity stacks (<=0.5 W) because PV conversion is ~50%; PV cells and windows are uni-fab buildable.

title: W: tungsten-free contactless probing raises known-good-die for HBM
idea: Replace W/Re needle probe cards (China ~80% of tungsten) with inductive/capacitive coupling coils placed in the scribe line and die I/O, so DRAM core wafers are tested at full speed without touching pads, enabling at-speed known-good-die screening before stacking.
why: HBM yield (fact 6) and scarce resources: at-speed KGD could halve the 20-30% stack yield loss and removes a tungsten dependency plus pad damage that hurts hybrid bonding.

title: FB-DIMM fixed: passive WDM optical bus, each module drops its own color
idea: FB-DIMM died because every Advanced Memory Buffer had to retime and re-drive all downstream traffic (4-6 W per DIMM, plus latency per hop). Replace the daisy chain with a motherboard waveguide carrying one wavelength per module: a passive ring filter on each module drops only its own wavelength and adds replies on a paired one, so no module repeats another's traffic and every slot sees the same latency.
why: Capacity per channel beyond DDR5's 1-2 DIMMs-per-channel electrical limit: 8-16 modules per channel at constant latency with ~5x lower buffer power than AMB, raising usable memory per socket.

title: Alignment-free nanopillar film gives tenfold interconnect density
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. A directed-self-assembly block-copolymer membrane filled with 30 nm vertical copper pillars at 60 nm pitch joins any pad to the facing pad with no precision alignment, because every pad lands on hundreds of pillars.
why: Interconnect density: pads shrink from 9 um to ~1 um pitch without $5-10M hybrid-bond aligners, ~10-80x more vertical wires per mm2 at the same tool cost.

title: Lane-direction-reconfigurable PHY for read-heavy phases
idea: Reverse fixed DQ symmetry: each lane has a transmitter and a receiver at both ends and can be reassigned in microseconds, so during LLM decode ~90% of lanes point memory-to-host and they flip back for checkpoint writes; per-burst bus turnaround disappears.
why: Recovers the ~10-15% bandwidth lost to read/write turnarounds and gives up to ~1.8x effective read bandwidth in read-dominated phases (fact 5).

title: Sense-amp-direct bonding: logic reads subarray stripes without global I/O
idea: Invert 'data must leave through global I/O, serializers and pads': hybrid-bond a logic die so every subarray's local sense-amp stripe has ~1 um-pitch bond pads directly above it and logic consumes row buffers in place.
why: Kills global dataline/serializer energy and much periphery; a full 8 Kb row is usable per activation instead of 64 b, erasing the 128x overfetch waste and approaching ~0.02-0.05 pJ/bit transport.

title: Wafer-on-wafer DRAM-on-logic accelerators with no package wiring
idea: Worsen: dice wafers, then reconnect chips with long package wires on CTE-mismatched substrates. Flip: hybrid-bond a whole DRAM wafer onto a whole logic wafer (all silicon, CTE-matched) with redundant tiles, so every logic tile has its own memory slab above it and package-level interconnect disappears.
why: Data movement (~0.05 pJ/bit vertical) and packaging cost: no interposer, no HBM base dies, no TSV stacks; yield handled by tile redundancy.

title: Dry-pack foundry business for water-stressed U.S. regions
idea: Box: customer memory dies x any x any x SAB, ACF or inductive stacking x glass or thermoplastic carriers x laser, plasma and dry-film steps only. A U.S. contract packager built with no UPW plant at all, offering memory stacking where wet fabs cannot get water rights, on cheaper land with faster permits.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: skips $100M+ UPW and wastewater plants, ~10-20x less water, and saves years of permitting.

title: Liquid-metal microchannel interconnects for reworkable memory-on-logic stacks
idea: Combine microfluidic channels with interconnect: a thin glass spacer with fiber-laser-drilled holes filled with gallium-indium eutectic sits between electroless Ni-P/Au barrier pads on memory and logic, so joints form at room temperature without plasma or bonding gases and a memory die can be removed and replaced.
why: Stacking yield and lifetime: rework recovers nearly all stacking yield loss and makes memory field-upgradable; rare-gas-free assembly.

title: Shingled solar-cell stacking: staircase DRAM dies with adhesive edge joints
idea: Adapted from shingled PV modules: DRAM dies are stacked offset like roof shingles so each die's pad row stays exposed, and each step is joined with dispensed electrically conductive adhesive instead of wire bonds or TSVs.
why: Low-capital stacking with no TSV etch or hybrid bonder, using 1990s dispensing robots; cost per stacked GB could fall 2-3x versus TSV HBM for capacity tiers.

title: Passive optical multicast feeds one weight copy to many accelerators
idea: Worsen: give each of 8-72 GPUs its own private HBM copy of the same model weights. Flip: keep one copy in a pooled memory appliance and broadcast weight streams through passive 1:32 optical splitters, so every accelerator receives the same layer at once and holds only activations and KV locally.
why: Usable supply: weight replication (often 50-80% of inference HBM) shrinks by the fan-out factor, freeing HBM for KV cache.

title: Sacrificial shorting bar removes ESD circuits from bonded links
idea: Po: memory with no protection. One top-metal mask adds a shorting bar that grounds every die-to-die pad during handling and bonding, then is laser-cut after assembly, so the I/O needs no ESD diodes.
why: ESD structures add area and pad capacitance; removing them cuts PHY area and per-bit link energy 20-40%.

title: Stethoscope: ultrasonic bulk-acoustic links replace TSVs vertically
idea: From the 'stethoscope': ScAlN piezo transducers on each thinned die launch GHz bulk acoustic pulses straight through the stack, and each tier listens with a resonator tuned to its own frequency (acoustic FDM). Vertical signaling then needs no copper via.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss); removes TSV keep-out zones and the TSV reveal/fill steps.

title: Hadamard-spread embedding storage turns bit flips into faint Gaussian noise
idea: Shift the unit of meaning from bits to whole vectors: embeddings are stored after a fixed Hadamard rotation and spread-spectrum quantization, so any 1% of flipped bits perturb every coordinate slightly instead of wrecking a few; the inverse transform runs in the near-memory logic die as data streams out.
why: Lets the largest AI capacity consumers (recommendation tables, retrieval indexes, KV caches) live in no-ECC 1%-BER memory with negligible accuracy loss, ~2x lower cost per usable bit.

title: Mycologist's fungal network: package-level HBM pooling crossbar
idea: Mycelium lends nutrients between trees: route a switched crossbar through the interposer so that, in a multi-die package, any compute die can borrow idle capacity in a neighbour die's HBM stacks with a one-hop ~5 ns penalty.
why: Reduces stranded HBM (often 20-30% idle per device), so fewer stacks are bought per unit of useful capacity.

title: Choir: frequency-multiplexed mm-wave carriers share each TSV
idea: Like a choir singing different notes on one stage: each TSV carries 4 mm-wave carriers with on-die mixers and filters, so one via does the work of four.
why: HBM TSV count and keep-out area cut about 4x, recovering part of the ~3x area-per-bit HBM tax.

title: Capacitive proximity coupling makes memory tiles reworkable, not bonded
idea: Box: 1T1C DRAM tile x standard access x charge-domain receiver x capacitive pads at 15 um pitch across a 1 um gap x spring-clamped Si carrier x no bump, no bond. Memory tiles are clamped face-down over the logic chip's pad field and talk through capacitive coupling, so a failing tile is unclipped and swapped instead of scrapping a $30k package.
why: HBM yield loss (fact 6): known-good package becomes field-replaceable, recovering the 20-30% stack and assembly scrap and allowing graded tiles; link ~0.2 pJ/bit.

title: Memory dies stand on edge like books on logic
idea: Box: DRAM die x standard x standard x sidewall-metallized edge bond at 20 um pitch x logic die as the shelf x laser-patterned sidewall plating. Thin DRAM dies are diced, edge-metallized and stood vertically in rows on the base logic die, so stack height no longer limits die count and each die's top edge touches the cold plate.
why: TSV tax and thermal ceiling of tall stacks: zero TSVs, 32+ dies per footprint row each with a direct heat path; bandwidth scales with edge length.

title: Cartographer's contour map: exponent-dedupe compression in base die
idea: A map keeps contours, not every pebble: the HBM base die stores and sends AI tensors as per-block shared exponents plus mantissa deltas (BF16/FP8 exponent dedupe), and decompresses at the controller, so fewer bits cross the TSVs and PHY.
why: Claimed 25-40% fewer bits moved and stored for weights and KV-cache, so effective capacity and bandwidth per stack rise by the same factor.

title: Self-folding micro-origami antennas for sub-THz wireless memory links
idea: Strain-mismatched metal bilayers on a 130 nm SiGe die curl up into 3D vertical dipoles and horn antennas when released, like self-folding origami. Memory chips then broadcast to compute across the board without package pins.
why: Wireless memory buses cut pin count and package cost and allow one-to-many broadcast; all mature-node.

title: Silicon-core vias: trench-isolated die silicon replaces copper TSV fill
idea: Substitute copper-filled TSVs with pillars of the die's own heavily doped silicon, isolated by an oxide-filled annular deep trench, so there is no copper CTE mismatch and the stress keep-out around each via largely disappears.
why: Fact 6: keep-out zones are a big part of TSV area; removing Cu stress shrinks them several-fold and drops Cu plating/CMP steps; suited to many slow parallel lanes.

title: Frequency-multiplexed RF carriers sharing each TSV
idea: Po: one wire, many voices. Each TSV carries four RF carriers (5-20 GHz) from tiny on-die oscillators and mixers, and each die listens through its own band-pass filter, so one TSV does the work of four and bandwidth can be reassigned between dies on the fly.
why: Cuts signal TSV count ~4x and recovers keep-out-zone area, shrinking the HBM TSV area tax.

title: Ti: NiTi shape-memory micro-clamps make HBM stacks test-then-commit
idea: Pattern sputtered NiTi micro-spring fingers on interposer pads that stay open at room temperature and clamp onto HBM microbump arrays when warmed past Af (~70 C); the whole package is run at speed while clamped, bad stacks are released by cooling and swapped, and only then is permanent underfill/reflow committed.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): today one bad stack scraps a package carrying 8 stacks plus a GPU; demountable test-before-commit could recover most of the 20-30% compound yield loss, effectively +15-25% HBM supply.

title: Seed library: open-source memory PHY and controller for U.S. startups
idea: Like a seed library lending seeds: fund an open-source LPDDR/UCIe-memory PHY and controller, silicon-proven on an open U.S. MPW, so U.S. chiplet and memory startups skip $5-10M IP licenses.
why: U.S. manufacturability and barriers to entry; more teams can build memory-side chiplets and new interfaces.

title: IBM MXT fixed: compression lives in the CXL link, not the core
idea: IBM's Memory eXpansion Technology (2000) doubled effective capacity with hardware compression but died from decompression latency on the CPU critical path, a large L3 requirement and OS changes. Put a 2-4 ns base-delta/zero-run compressor with a metadata cache inside the CXL memory controller, present the OS a fixed larger capacity, and compress only far-tier lines so hot data never pays the latency.
why: Do DRAM's job with less, and link energy: server data typically compresses 1.5-2.5x, so 33-60% fewer DRAM bits for the same capacity and fewer bits crossing the link.

title: Cotton-candy electrospun nanofiber dielectric for interposer wiring
idea: Electrospin polyimide nanofiber mats, like spinning cotton candy, to form a mostly-air interlayer dielectric with k around 1.4 around interposer memory traces.
why: Wire capacitance falls ~2x, so CV^2 I/O energy per bit falls ~40% on 2.5D memory links.

title: Trench-DRAM revival: HBr/Cl2 deep-trench etch makes fluorine-free TSVs
idea: Repurpose the abandoned IBM/Siemens/Qimonda trench-capacitor deep-silicon etch (HBr/O2/Cl2, AR ~50:1) to etch 5 x 30 um TSVs in thinned DRAM, with SiBrxOy sidewall passivation in place of Bosch fluorocarbon polymer.
why: Constraint: TSVs without SF6 (the strongest greenhouse gas) or PFAS-class C4F8, reusing existing deep-trench know-how; slower (~1 um/min) etch is the cost, offset by thinner dies (fact 6).

title: Deferred linear correction: compute on raw weights, subtract error product later
idea: Exploit matmul linearity to shift correction in time: the accelerator multiplies immediately with raw 1%-BER weights (exponent bits ride in a protected lane), while the decoder later emits a sparse error matrix E, and the output is fixed by subtracting E*x at ~1-2% of the original work.
why: Removes ~10-20 ns of decode latency from every HBM read and lets cheap 1%-BER cells feed accelerators at full speed.

title: Boron-arsenide interlayers let HBM stacks grow to 24 dies
idea: Box: HBM die x standard x standard x hybrid bond with 2 um cubic BAs or CVD-diamond interlayers plus thermal vias x Si x low-temperature deposition. Ultra-high-conductivity interlayers spread heat sideways to dedicated thermal through-vias so 24-high stacks stay under 85 C.
why: Bits per package footprint: +50% capacity per stack site without new shoreline; cooler dies also need less refresh.

title: Acoustic bus: GHz sound waves through stacked silicon
idea: Po: memory talks by sound. Thin-film AlScN transducers on every die launch and detect 3-10 GHz bulk acoustic pulses that propagate vertically through the bonded silicon stack, carrying command, address and refresh-sync broadcasts with no TSV at all.
why: Frees all command/address TSVs for data and broadcasts to every die in one shot; trims TSV count and periphery.

title: Via-ROM weight chiplet: frozen weights need no DRAM
idea: Eliminate DRAM, its writes and its refresh for deployed model weights: encode weights in a single custom via-mask layer of a mature-node ROM die (one via = one bit) hybrid-bonded under the compute die; the data survives power loss by construction.
why: Weights are ~60-80% of inference memory; via-ROM is ~5x cheaper per bit than DRAM, needs one 28-40 nm mask (no EUV, U.S.-fabbable) and reads at ~0.1 pJ/bit over hybrid bonds.

title: Laser-coded material tags plus memory take-back policy
idea: MINIFY sorting cost: every memory package carries a laser-etched material bill of Cu/Sn/Si/Au, read by automated shredder lines, under an extended-producer-responsibility rule for DRAM.
why: U.S. scarce-resource recovery: makes recycled Cu, Sn and Au streams economic and gives domestic secondary supply.

title: Implant body-channel trick: send memory data over power planes
idea: Implants use the body itself as the wire (intra-body communication). Superimpose low-amplitude multi-GHz carriers on the stack's power/ground TSV network and separate them on each die with on-die band-pass filters, so power TSVs double as data channels.
why: Power and ground take a large share of HBM TSVs and bumps; reusing them adds ~1.5-2x signal capacity without more TSVs, easing the TSV tax.

title: Card catalog: base-die Bloom filters answer misses before crossing link
idea: Like a library card catalog: the HBM/CXL memory base die keeps Bloom-filter catalogs of key-value and embedding tables, so a lookup that would miss is answered 'absent' without moving data across the link or opening a row.
why: Destructive-read and overfetch energy (fact 8) for sparse lookups; cuts 20-50% of wasted activations in recommendation and retrieval workloads.

title: Append-only log port built for KV-cache streaming
idea: The long-context KV cache is an extreme user: written once per token, appended sequentially, read whole every step. Add a port mode with a hardware append pointer (writes carry no address) and descriptor-driven sequential read streams, so command/address traffic, row-conflict scheduling and refresh collisions largely vanish for that region.
why: Cuts CA pins ~60% and lifts bus efficiency from ~70% to ~95% for KV traffic; ~30% more bandwidth per pin without new cells.

title: Silicon transparency: infrared optical vias broadcast commands through HBM stacks
idea: Silicon is transparent above 1.1 um, so a 1.3 um VCSEL on the base die shines vertically through 16 thinned DRAM dies, each carrying a small partially absorbing Ge photoconductor window that taps ~5% of the light; command/address and clock are broadcast optically to all dies at once instead of through TSV columns.
why: Removes C/A and clock TSVs and their capacitive load (facts 5, 6); one emitter replaces 16 drivers; ~30-40% fewer TSVs, sub-pJ/bit broadcast.

title: Tailor's made-to-measure: maskless late-binding RDL after die test
idea: A tailor cuts after measuring: mount mass-produced memory chiplets loosely, test them, then write the interposer RDL wiring per package with direct-write laser lithography, routing around dead dies and binning good banks into full channels.
why: Removes interposer mask sets and rescues partially failing dies (HBM yield loss 20-30%); claimed 10-15% more usable bits per wafer.

title: Mg: magnesium-silicide thermoelectric micro-coolers spot-cool HBM PHY
idea: Integrate thin-film Mg2Si/Mg3Sb2 Peltier elements (abundant, tellurium-free alternative to Bi2Te3) in the HBM lid over the hottest base-die PHY region, actively pumping 5-10 W/cm2 during bursts so the stack never crosses 85 C; control is local and the interface unchanged.
why: Refresh and throttling (fact 3): avoids 2x refresh and thermal throttling at peak load using abundant elements with no Te/China chokepoint.

title: Newspaper web press: roll-to-roll nanoimprinted flex interposer film
idea: Run polyimide film through a roll-to-roll line like a newspaper press: a nickel roller stamp nanoimprints 2 um wiring trenches, slot-die coats seed, and electroplating fills them at metres per minute. The film is then laminated under HBM stacks and the GPU instead of a silicon interposer.
why: Attacks CoWoS/silicon interposer capacity and cost; claims ~5-10x lower interposer cost per mm2 and continuous rather than wafer-batch throughput.

title: Space-solar Miura fold turns one thin DRAM sheet into a stack
idea: Adapted from Miura-ori folding of satellite solar arrays: a strip of DRAM dies is built on an ultra-thin flexible bonded film with continuous copper traces across the fold lines. The strip folds accordion-style into a 16-high stack whose wires wrap around the folds instead of passing through TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSVs, their keep-out and per-tier bonding steps, targeting ~20% lower stack cost and higher yield.

title: Active interposer swallows DRAM periphery; arrays go periphery-light
idea: Invert 'periphery lives on the memory die': make the interposer in a U.S. 65-90 nm fab carrying upper decoder levels, refresh control, ECC and repeaters, while hybrid-bonded DRAM dies keep only sense amps and local drivers.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die; moving half onto cheap mature silicon lifts array efficiency toward 70-75%, ~1.4x bits per DRAM wafer.

title: Plastic sub-terahertz waveguide ribbons link memory without lasers
idea: Scarcity: no lasers, and copper cannot reach beyond 10 cm. 140-300 GHz CMOS transceivers couple into polymer dielectric waveguides (PTFE/HDPE ribbons) linking memory modules to processors over 0.1-2 m at 50-100 Gb/s per strand.
why: Disaggregation energy (fact 5): pooled memory at ~1-3 pJ/bit with plastic media and CMOS-only transceivers, no III-V lasers.

title: Desert architect's double roof: thermal-break gap between memory and logic
idea: Desert dwellers use a ventilated double roof: suspend the DRAM stack over a 5-10 um vacuum gap above the 150 C+ logic die, couple signals across the gap by near-field coupling, and feed power from the board side through separate thermal-choke ribbons.
why: Keeps DRAM at the 125 C ambient instead of logic's 150-170 C junction, cutting refresh about 4-8x and ending retention-driven bandwidth loss.

title: Light-powered contactless self-test of bare memory dies
idea: Substitute probe-card test with optical test: each die carries a tiny photovoltaic cell and LED; a light flash powers on-die BIST and the die blinks its pass/fail and repair map to a camera, testing thousands of dies in parallel without contact.
why: Fact 6 yield and W chokepoint: contactless known-good-die test cuts test cost and probe damage, making test-before-stack cheap.

title: Gravure-offset printed fan-out redistribution layers on panels
idea: Borrow gravure-offset printing from printed electronics: an engraved cylinder inks silver/copper nanoparticle lines at 5 um width onto a blanket and transfers them to fan-out panels at about 1 m/s. Use it for the coarse layers that route memory base dies to the package.
why: Cuts capital and step count for the coarse RDL that makes up most layers; claims ~10x lower capex per layer.

title: Ship untested wafers: skip hours-long retention test and burn-in
idea: Shift testing from the fab's hours-long retention screens and burn-in ovens to the field's nanosecond decoder: wafers go from light probe straight to bonding, and the base die learns per-row error statistics online.
why: Test and burn-in cost ~5-10% of cost per bit and weeks of cycle time; dropping them frees test-floor capital and speeds supply.

title: Local quality: tapered TSV stacks, fewer TSVs in each higher tier
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: in a uniform HBM stack every die carries the full TSV farm, though the top die needs none. One common front-side mask lays out the TSV farm region as spare subarrays, and a cheap i-line backside mask per tier etches only the TSVs that die needs for the dies above it. In upper tiers the unetched subarrays are fused on as extra capacity.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): average TSV area per die drops ~45% in a 12-high stack, for ~5-10% more bits per stack with the same front-side masks.

title: Bit-significance stack: MSB planes on clean dies, LSB planes on cheap dies
idea: Shift the unit of placement from the word to the bit-plane along the stack's vertical axis: sign, exponent and high-mantissa planes go to 4 protected dies, low-order planes go to 8 dies running at 1% BER with no ECC, and the base die re-interleaves planes into words on the fly.
why: Two-thirds of bits live on refresh-relaxed, low-voltage dies (facts 3, 10) with <0.1% model-quality loss; precision-on-demand fetching also cuts data moved up to ~50%.

title: XOR-delta writes: send only the changed bytes
idea: MINIFY write traffic: the base die keeps the old cache line, the host sends only the nonzero bytes of new XOR old plus a bitmask, and the base die patches the row with a masked write.
why: Data-movement energy and write bandwidth: optimizer, gradient and KV updates are often sparse in bytes; claims 2-4x less write traffic.

title: Window-glass trick: vertical infrared optical bus through silicon stack
idea: Silicon is as clear at 1310 nm as window glass is to sunlight. A laser array on the base die shines straight up through the thinned die stack. Every tier has resonant-cavity detectors tuned to its own wavelength, so each takes only its channel and lets the rest pass. Return traffic uses modulated retroreflectors.
why: Replaces thousands of signal TSVs (behind HBM's ~3x area/bit and its stacking yield loss) with a few optical columns. Targets <1 pJ/bit vertical links and 30-50% less TSV keep-out area.

title: Progressive-JPEG bit-plane memory with early-stop streaming
idea: Progressive JPEG sends coarse detail first, then fine. Store tensors bit-plane-transposed so a burst returns the MSBs of many values first. The consumer (attention scoring, vector search) ends the stream once it has enough precision, and fetches low bit-planes only for the top-k survivors.
why: Attention and similarity search need full precision on only a few entries. MSB-first fetch could cut bits moved for KV-cache and embedding reads 2-4x.

title: Bit-plane-major storage with progressive-precision fetch
idea: Rearrange bit order: weights are stored transposed so that each DRAM burst holds the same bit position of 512 different weights. The accelerator fetches the top 4 bit-planes first and fetches lower planes only for layers or tokens whose error estimate needs them.
why: Facts 5 and 8: inference moves 2-4x fewer bytes on average at near-equal accuracy, multiplying effective bandwidth and turning precision into a runtime knob instead of a stored format.

title: Artist's negative space: SRAM-filled grout bridges between chiplets
idea: An artist paints the empty gaps: fill the 100-500 um dead gaps between HBM stacks and the GPU with thin silicon 'grout' bridge strips that hold repeaters plus 2-8 MB of line-buffer SRAM, so the gap becomes a staging cache and a retiming point.
why: Uses wasted interposer area to absorb bursty traffic and cut DRAM activations (128x overfetch) by ~20%; lower-swing, shorter wire hops cut interface pJ/bit.

title: Lego: double-sided commodity LPDDR around FPGA as poor man's HBM
idea: Like Lego bricks: stock LPDDR5X packages are placed on both sides of a thin, short-trace substrate directly around an FPGA or accelerator die, with 16 or more channels in parallel, using a standard OSAT build. A demo module fits within $1M.
why: HBM TSV tax and supply; HBM-class aggregate bandwidth from commodity non-HBM DRAM at ~1/3 the cost per bit.

title: Compute on top, memory underneath, power through the stack
idea: Reverse HBM's placement: the accelerator die sits on top of a DRAM stack next to the heat sink, dense power-TSV columns through every DRAM die feed it, and the memory interface becomes a direct face-to-back hybrid bond into the top DRAM die.
why: Removes interposer beachfront and HBM PHYs (facts 5, 6): ~10 TB/s per cm2 of vertical bandwidth at ~0.1 pJ/bit, and the usual memory-on-logic thermal problem is avoided because logic sits next to the cooler.

title: LCD-fab panel interposers on Gen-8 display glass
idea: Display backplanes are made on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass at ≤350 C. Convert idle LCD/TFT lines to pattern multi-layer Cu RDL (2 um L/S) and through-glass vias on full panels, then cut the panels into HBM interposers. Every step stays ≤350 C.
why: A panel has ~70x the area of a 300 mm wafer. Interposer cost per mm² could fall 5-10x, and CoWoS-class capacity could be added in existing display lines, including U.S. conversions.

title: Sauce-reduction gradient summing inside the HBM base die
idea: A sauce is reduced in the pot before it is served. An adder array in the HBM base die likewise sums incoming gradient shards from several GPUs in place, with read-add-write inside the stack. Only reduced tensors cross the interposer.
why: All-reduce sends each gradient byte across links about twice. Reducing in the stack halves link traffic and the 3-4 pJ/bit HBM PHY energy for training.

title: Goodyear STARAN revival: multidimensional-access memory serves bit-planes on demand
idea: Revive STARAN's 1972 multi-dimensional-access memory: a flip-network permutation in the HBM base die lets one stored array be read word-wise or bit-plane-wise, so precision-adaptive kernels fetch only the top k bit-planes of weights or activations.
why: Facts 5/8: fetching 4 of 16 bit-planes moves 4x fewer bits for draft, speculative or early-exit passes, without storing duplicate low-precision copies (saves capacity too).

title: Vector-quantized KV cache sized to fit base-die SRAM
idea: Ideal: the working set shrinks until static memory can hold it. Closest achievable: the base die encodes each KV vector as 2-4 indices into learned per-head codebooks (product quantization), shrinking the KV cache 8-16x so the hot cache fits in base-die SRAM, and computes attention scores directly on the codes.
why: Zero refresh power for the KV tier and 8-16x less KV traffic (fact 5); KV cache is the fastest-growing DRAM consumer in long-context inference.

title: Sous-vide nanotwinned copper hybrid bonding at 150 C
idea: Sous vide reaches doneness at low temperature over a long time. Electroplate (111)-oriented nanotwinned Cu pads, whose fast surface diffusion lets Cu-Cu hybrid bonds form at 150 C over several hours in batch ovens.
why: Lower bond temperature cuts warpage and stress. That permits thinner dies and finer pitch (<3 um) for memory-on-logic, and protects heat-sensitive memory layers.

title: Solderless nano-velcro interconnect makes HBM socketable and reworkable
idea: Eliminate solder and permanent bonding: grow interlocking copper nanohook forests on memory and logic pads (~5 um pitch) that mesh mechanically at room temperature under clamp pressure and can be unclipped; a failed or outgrown stack is swapped instead of scrapping a $30k GPU package.
why: HBM package yield loss (20-30%) compounds over 8 stacks; reworkability recovers most of it and lets memory be sold/upgraded separately from compute, claimed ~15-25% lower effective cost/bit.

title: Dual-ported HBM shared by neighboring GPUs ends stranded capacity
idea: Eliminate fixed one-GPU ownership of HBM: a base die with two PHYs links a stack to two adjacent GPU packages via a bridge, so capacity flows to whichever GPU needs it (KV cache on one, weights on the other).
why: Fleet HBM utilization is often 50-70%; pairwise pooling recovers ~15-25% capacity, so fewer DRAM bits are bought per useful bit.

title: Phone-filter piezo transducers send ultrasonic data vertically through stacks
idea: Adapted from AlN bulk-acoustic-wave filters in smartphones: thin piezo transducers on each die launch GHz acoustic pulses through the bonded silicon stack to receivers on other dies. Data TSVs are replaced by frequency- or time-multiplexed acoustic channels.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): could remove ~1-2k data TSVs per die and their keep-out zones, leaving only bonding and power vias.

title: Climate-model halo links: memory stacks talk directly to neighbors
idea: Weather codes are dominated by halo exchange between neighboring domains. Add short serial side-links from each HBM base die to the nearest stack of the adjacent GPU, so halos, KV pages and pipeline activations migrate memory-to-memory without crossing either GPU's PHY and NoC.
why: Halves PHY crossings for inter-GPU transfers (each ~1-5 pJ/bit) and frees GPU I/O for compute traffic; lets neighboring GPUs pool capacity instead of duplicating it.

title: Fisherman's net: passive optical multicast of shared weights
idea: One net catches many fish: one memory chiplet's optical transmitter feeds a passive 1:8 splitter, so a shared weight tensor read once from DRAM reaches eight accelerators together instead of being duplicated in eight HBM stacks.
why: Cuts duplicated model copies across GPUs (common in inference serving): claimed 3-8x less DRAM capacity for weights, and one read's energy serves many consumers.

title: Slinky: helical micro-spring bonds absorb CTE mismatch
idea: Forced 'slinky': electroplated helical micro-springs at 10 um pitch connect silicon DRAM dies to large glass or organic panels and flex to absorb CTE mismatch, so large panels do not crack or warp joints.
why: Panel-level packaging cost; lets cheap large substrates replace silicon interposers for memory-rich modules.

title: Liquid-metal micro-sockets let interposers outlive three DRAM generations
idea: Shift packaging lifetime from one product cycle to a decade: HBM stacks seat into polymer wells filled with gallium-indium alloy at ~20 um pitch, held by a clamp, so stacks lift out at room temperature for swap, upgrade or redeployment. The costly logic die and interposer persist while memory rotates.
why: Raises effective supply and cuts embodied capital: good HBM is no longer scrapped with the accelerator, giving ~2-3x more service years per stack.

title: Gap-junction tiers: adjacent bonded array dies share sense amplifiers
idea: Array dies are hybrid-bonded face-to-face at bitline-group pitch so that one sense-amplifier and column layer sits between them and serves bitlines from the die above and the die below, like gap junctions joining the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells. Each pair of array dies carries one periphery instead of two.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): sharing sense-amp and column circuits across two arrays halves periphery per bit, roughly 25% more bits per mm^2 of stack.

title: Phone BAW-filter acoustic data links through the stack
idea: Phones filter RF with sputtered AlN bulk-acoustic-wave resonators deposited at ≤350 C. Put ScAlN transducer pairs on each thinned DRAM die so GHz ultrasound carries data straight up through the silicon. Channels are frequency-multiplexed, and each tier picks off its own.
why: Removes signal TSVs, their keep-out zones and their yield loss. Even 10-20 acoustic channels per mm² at 5-10 Gb/s would replace a large share of HBM signal TSVs.

title: Micro-HBM carpet: dozens of tiny stacks over the die
idea: Eliminate the beachfront limit and interposer distance: instead of 8 large edge stacks, hybrid-bond ~64 small 4-high 1-2 GB stacks directly over the compute die's area with thermal pillars between them, each feeding the tile beneath it.
why: Wire length drops from ~5 mm to ~50 um and IO energy from 3-4 to ~0.2 pJ/bit; 4-high stacks yield far better than 12-high and need no interposer.

title: Navy signalman's heliograph: optical retromodulator backscatter from memory
idea: A signalman flashes a mirror instead of carrying a lamp: the cool-side controller shines a beam onto the memory chiplet, which sends data back by switching an electro-absorption retroreflector, so the hot memory side has no laser and very little transmit power.
why: No laser in the 125 C package and almost no transmit heat on the memory side; claimed ~0.2 pJ/bit on the memory end of the link.

title: Gallium liquid-metal microbumps in micro-wells
idea: MINIFY the melting point to ~30 C: microbumps are galinstan-filled wells capped by a dielectric frame, so a die lifts off with gentle heat and reseats with the wells reformed.
why: Rework and recycling of stacked memory; dies come out clean with no solder residue, cutting scrap and tin use.

title: DRAM bonded onto the backside of compute
idea: MINIFY vertical distance to ~10 um by hybrid-bonding DRAM to the back face of a backside-power-delivery logic wafer, with nano-vias interleaved with the power grid, so memory sits directly under every compute core.
why: Data-movement energy (HBM 3-4 pJ/bit): claims ~0.1 pJ/bit and removes the interposer entirely.

title: Persistent glass memory backplane with consumable compute
idea: MAGNIFY substrate life: DRAM is embedded in cavities of a long-lived glass-core backplane, and compute chiplets land on top through reversible bumps and are swapped every generation.
why: Capital intensity: memory, the expensive scarce part, is installed once and serves many compute upgrades.

title: Aligned-particle conductive film attaches memory without flux or washing
idea: Box: DRAM die x standard x standard x anisotropic conductive film with magnetically aligned Ni-Au particles at 10 um pitch x organic or glass substrate x dry thermocompression. One press bonds the die, forms the underfill and makes every contact, eliminating flux, aqueous post-reflow wash and capillary underfill.
why: Water: flux cleaning and underfill prep dominate die-attach water; ACF is dry, >10x less water, and faster.

title: CHIPS packaging grants gated on litres-per-gigabyte water budgets
idea: Box: any memory x any access x any sensing x any packaging route x U.S. sites x dry toolsets required. Federal packaging incentives require metered packaging water intensity of 0.1 L/GB or less, with bonus credit for dry steps such as laser dicing, SAB, ACF and dry resist.
why: Water and U.S. manufacturability: lets packaging plants get permits in water-stressed Arizona and Texas, forces 10x cuts and creates a U.S. market for dry tools.

title: Venus alien: SiC CMOS base die and memory PHY
idea: For a Venusian 125 C is cold: build the HBM base die and PHY in SiC CMOS (developed for 500 C Venus probes), whose 3.3 eV bandgap keeps leakage negligible at 125 C and whose ~370 W/mK conductivity spreads heat away from the DRAM layers.
why: Hot periphery leakage and timing drift at 125 C go away, and DRAM layers run ~10 C cooler (about 2x less refresh); I/O energy stays flat over temperature.

title: Row-scale LDPC: decode the whole 8 KB activated row at once
idea: Shift the ECC codeword from 64 bits to the 64 Kb row that activation already drags out: a rate-0.85 LDPC code spans each row and a pipeline in the base die decodes it as the row lands in the buffer. A 1% raw cell BER drops below 1e-15 with ~15% parity (BSC capacity at 1% is 0.92).
why: Turns 128x overfetch (fact 8) into an asset; tolerating 1% BER permits ~4-8x longer refresh (fact 3) and smaller capacitors (fact 1).

title: Million-token agents: attention scoring inside the HBM base die
idea: Million-token agent contexts make decode almost pure KV reads. The base die streams keys internally at full TSV bandwidth, computes low-precision q.k scores, and returns only the top-k keys' values plus a residual over the PHY.
why: For long contexts only ~1-5% of values need to cross the interface; PHY energy per logical token access drops 10-20x and HBM bandwidth stops bounding decode.

title: Deep-trench eDRAM chiplet mosaic from U.S. logic fabs
idea: Invert 'bandwidth must come from dense commodity DRAM': tile 16-32 small deep-trench eDRAM chiplets (IBM-heritage process at GlobalFoundries New York) around the accelerator as a hot tier for activations and KV, packaged in the U.S.
why: Density is ~10x below DRAM, but edge bandwidth and ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit make it a bandwidth-not-capacity tier, trimming hot-data HBM need 20-40% using domestic fabs that exist today.

title: Shape-memory polymer: printed thermally releasable underfill makes chiplet modules reworkable
idea: Print an underfill made of shape-memory epoxy that is rigid and stress-relieving below 120 C but softens and contracts past a 160 C transition, so a failed memory chiplet can be lifted off a printed interposer and replaced.
why: Chiplet package yield and scrap (fact 6): reworkability saves the whole module; thermal-cycling reliability must be proven.

title: Edge-standing die library: DRAM dies stood upright
idea: MAGNIFY dies per footprint by standing 100 thin DRAM dies upright like books, each bonded on one polished edge to the substrate through edge pads, with coolant flowing in the gaps between them.
why: Removes TSVs entirely and multiplies capacity per footprint about 10x versus a flat layout, with cooling built in.

title: Memory leasing with guaranteed take-back and refurbishment
idea: MINIFY ownership: vendors lease HBM and CXL modules, take them back at end of term, refurbish and redeploy them, which gives them a financial reason to design for disassembly.
why: Effective supply and capital: each module serves 2-3 lifecycles; cuts buyer capex at a time when prices have risen 4x.

title: On-die health passport for second-life grading
idea: MAGNIFY what each die knows about its own history: an on-die tamper-proof log of power-on hours, ECC events, row-hammer counts and temperature lets refurbishers grade stacks instantly.
why: Second-life supply: cheap trustworthy grading makes reused DRAM sellable, adding usable bits without new fabs.

title: Defective DRAM arrays recycled as flying capacitors for regulators
idea: Box: failed 1T1C sub-arrays x wordlines held on x no sensing (capacitor bank) x in-stack switched-capacitor converter x each DRAM die x fuse-programmed at test. Sub-arrays that fail test are fused into parallel banks (5 fF x millions = tens of nF) that act as flying caps for an on-die 4:1 converter, so the stack accepts 4 V input on far fewer power TSVs.
why: Yield and TSV tax (fact 6): turns scrap area into function, cuts power TSVs and bumps ~4x through higher input voltage, and lowers I2R loss.

title: Inductive-coil stacks held by removable adhesive
idea: MINIFY the metallurgical bond to zero: dies talk through on-chip inductor coils, are stacked with a reworkable adhesive, and a failed die is peeled out and replaced with no bumps to reflow.
why: Removes TSVs and the HBM TSV tax; repairable stacks recover the 20-30% yield loss as rework instead of scrap.

title: Panel-scale glass interposers replacing reticle-stitched silicon
idea: Ideal: interposers as cheap as window glass. Closest achievable: build redistribution layers and through-glass vias on 510x515 mm glass panels with LCD-style lithography, giving ~6x the area per process pass of a 300 mm wafer with flatness good enough for 2 um lines.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: reuses display tools and domestic glass supply; interposer cost per package falls ~3-5x and the reticle-size limit disappears, allowing more HBM sites per GPU.

title: Backscatter chiplet links: memory dies reflect a shared mm-wave carrier
idea: Combine RFID backscatter with in-package interconnect: the host radiates one 60-300 GHz carrier into a shielded package cavity and each memory die switches the impedance of a small on-die antenna to reflect its data; memory dies need no oscillator, PA or bump field for data.
why: Data-movement energy and assembly: transmit energy at the memory die ~0.1 pJ/bit; dies can sit unbonded/swappable in the cavity, removing TSV/bond yield loss for capacity tiers.

title: Few fast TSVs: 16 Gb/s per TSV
idea: MAGNIFY the rate per TSV to ~16 Gb/s with tiny on-die serializers, so ~90% of HBM data TSVs disappear (about 100 per stack instead of ~1,000+).
why: HBM TSV tax and yield: TSV area and defect count fall about 10x; claims +15-20% stack yield.

title: NIC inside the HBM base die for direct remote writes
idea: Eliminate the GPU hop for network data: put a co-packaged optical RDMA engine in each HBM base die so remote nodes write KV caches, gradients and activations directly into the target stack without crossing the GPU's PHY and NoC twice.
why: Removes ~2 extra interface crossings per byte (~6-8 pJ/bit saved) and frees GPU beachfront from network SerDes for more memory.

title: Vinyl-pressing nanoimprint stamped RDL trenches and vias
idea: Records are pressed from a master. Likewise, UV-nanoimprint a reusable master into polymer dielectric at room temperature to form 0.5-1 um RDL trenches and via cups in one stroke. Electroplate Cu, then CMP, with a final cure ≤250 C.
why: A stamp replaces several litho exposures per RDL layer. That cuts interposer patterning capex ~3-5x and gives sub-um lines for wider memory buses.

title: Biologist's bloodstream: data riding on the stack's power rails
idea: Blood carries oxygen and nutrients in one vessel, so superimpose low-swing, high-frequency data (5-20 GHz OFDM tones) on the HBM power and ground TSVs, which already make up ~50% of TSVs, with on-die LC filters to separate the two.
why: Recovers TSV and bump budget so stacks need fewer dedicated signal TSVs: claimed 30-40% fewer total TSVs, or 1.5x bandwidth for the same TSV count, which cuts the TSV area tax.
